newsitem.title: USA: Con Edison settlement sets largest rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Con Edison settlement sets largest rate cut.

text.p: The New York Public Service Commission said a settlement reached with Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc proposes the largest rate cut in the state's history of electric utility regulation.
But Assembly Energy Committee Chairman Paul D. Tonko called the savings insignificant for consumers while large industrial power users costs are reduced 25 percent.
The commission said the settlement agreement in Con Edison's Competitive Opportunities rate and restructuring proceeding reduces power costs $1 billion over five years.
It said the immediate 25 percent reduction goes to industrial constomers with monthly demand in excess of 1,500 kilowatts.

The commission said its staff looked at providing equal rate reductions for all customer classes but rejected that option because the typical residential customer would gain less than $1 per month amnd the benefits to Con Edison customers of economic development would be eliminated.
The commission also noted the plan does notinclude projected savings from securitization of the utilities stranded costs.

If this plan is approved by the legislature, the savings could double rate decreases for residential and small commercial customers -- now 3.3 percent and 10 percent, respectively, over five years, the commission said.
Con Edison said the agreement gives it the "opportunity" to recover stranded costs through an undisclosed distribution charge that will be in place for five years.
Noting the "closed-door proceedings" that led to the agreement, Tonko said "it appears the scales are tipped to favor the utility shareholder rather than the consumer."

He said "stockholders, not consumers, must shoulder the primary burden for stranded assets. The benefits of reward are seated with the investor, and so is the price of risk. The consumer consumer is innocent and should not be viewed as providers of corporate insurance."

Tonko called the commission's version of competition "an illusion. Rather than a robust competitive market it appears the (Republican Gov. George) Pataki administration would prefer to stifle true consumer access."
The Democratic Assemblyman said "I believe we need to rewrite the archaic rules currently in place" for regulation of the electric utility industry.
